Firstly, the authorities in Kabul have made a request for international assistance and given the conditions in the country, they will welcome the international assistance. Number two, we are working, our partner on the ground is the Afghan Red Crescent and the Red Crescent across societies. Now, you must remember that the Afghan Red Crescent and the movement has been working with the Taliban even before they took office, even in the areas that were once controlled by the Taliban. So there's a good working relationship with the authorities understanding the role of the Red Cross Red Crescent that we bring humanitarian assistance. Given the status of the Afghan Red Crescent, which has a wide network of volunteers throughout the country, I'm very confident that we would be able to reach the communities that are affected by the earthquake without too much bureaucratic obstacles. How can they, should they want to offer any kind of aid to the people of Afghanistan who are suffering from this natural disaster? The Singapore Red Cross has launched a public appeal. We are hoping to reach out to Singaporeans who can contribute to contribute towards this appeal. In any disaster, the best is to be able to purchase these relief items either in the country itself, which means it will overcome all the freight costs and the customs clearances or in a country near the point of the disaster. So we want to urge people to come forward if they can to donate generously so that we will be able to assist the communities that are affected by the disaster. There are some people who want to donate in kind. You can approach us, but generally when we donate in kind, it's very difficult to get these items into the country unless they are new, unless they are in bulk. And we are able to facilitate this shipment. Thanks so much for joining us. Mr. Benjamin Williams, CEO of the Singapore Red Cross, on the race to send aid to disaster hit Afghanistan.

title: Singapore Red Cross to feature in NDP show segment for the first time this year
description: No longer just part of the March in Contingent, Singapore's Red Cross Society will be making its debut at the National Day Parade Show segment this year. To mark total defense, the hope is that everyday Singaporeans can step up to offer help in times of need. Claudia Lim goes behind the scenes. It's Saturday morning and although show time is several hours later, some 10 volunteers from the Red Cross are already preparing for rehearsals. This year, they're showing Singaporeans how they can play a part in defending the nation during an attack. Despite the different changes and the weekly sun tanning session, it has been a fulfilling journey meeting with new people and all. I think it's the mission of Red Cross that brings me to volunteer for this role and I think it is quite important to demonstrate such skills to the public. Through this total defense 40 segment, many people can find out what actually Red Cross does. Here you can see us in action. We are actually literally providing psychological first aid and I don't think many people have actually heard of psychological first aid. Using a simulated scenario where a bus was hijacked by terrorists, volunteers prepare to lend their helping hand to those in need. This may be a show, but it's a significant event for us where we get together and it actually reflects what we are supposed to do when a real crisis happens. When night falls, it's time for the volunteers to inspire Singaporeans. Volunteers from the Singapore Red Cross Society are assisting people in psychological first aid. Ms Chan says the hope is that Singaporeans can find roles for themselves according to their strengths and interests. Be it through crisis management, blood donation or helping youth and seniors.

title: Singapore Red Cross sends team to oversee medical aid distribution for Ukraine war victims
description: A team from the Singapore Red Cross is in Budapest, Hungary, to arrange for medical aid to victims of the Ukraine war using logistical corridors. Now, this is the first time the Singapore Red Cross is working in a war situation in Europe. Its previous aid missions have been mostly in Asia for victims of natural disasters. For more, Sahari Ani from the Singapore Red Cross joins us now from Hungary. Sahari, tell us more about the work that you're doing there in Hungary. Firstly, both of us, Karol and I, are now in Hungary for the past several weeks on a humanitarian mission to Ukraine-neighboring countries that are hosting a majority of the refugees that is Hungary, Lutinias, Slovakia and Poland. Our goal is to oversee the humanitarian response supported by the people of Singapore to Singapore's humanitarian efforts for the reunion and to explore further opportunities to expand our operations. Since our arrival in Budapest, we have conducted several meetings with our partners and we have visited a service operation location where our partners, the Hungarian Red Cross, have provided support to the transiting refugees in Budapest. And we were going to work closely with other humanitarian partners on the ground to identify and to support the other needs of the fast-growing refugee crisis. Sahari, the needs of the refugees who've come into Hungary and those other countries that you mentioned, they are multiple, they are complex. Give us a sense of how you're getting that aid across to the people who need it the most. A million of people are in needs of humanitarian assistance. Many of them have fled the countries and others have been internally de-placed. The Red Cross and the Recreation Movement has a comprehensive presence and a network of national societies either in Ukraine or the neighboring countries and they are able to mobilize and scale up the necessary resources. With these resources, thus far, we have delivered almost 1,200 megatons of its, half of which has been delivered to the Ukrainian Red Cross for distribution. These aid are delivered either by line through trucks or by air through airplanes, reaching more than 1 million people and further additional aids are in the pen line. Our colleagues also working in close contact with the Ukrainians in living in Singapore as well as Singaporeans living in and around Ukraine to facilitate our work on the ground. We need many helping hand and we are working closely with our Red Cross movement and humanitarian partners on the ground. So a sizable amount of aid getting through to the people who need it, but what are some of the most urgent needs or supplies required that you've seen, Sahari? The scale of the people movement is massive and it's still very free as it is influenced by the situation in Ukraine. The demographic of the displaced persons, the children, the older persons, the people with special needs, the impact, the physical and the psychological impact, the needs, the short term and the longer term. We also need to keep in mind that they, the Ukraine and the neighboring country are recovering from impact of COVID-19. These are intertwined factors that we need to consider as we try to comprehend and understand the challenges and need. Of course, decide supporting the immediate relief. We will continue to focus on addressing the basic needs such as emergency shelters, protection, health, water, sanitation, hygiene and psychosocial support. Our latest trash of medical aids reflect our priorities. This is to help the most vulnerable person including children and youth, women with infant and young children, the elderly and the patient with rare diseases and persons with disabilities. A complex and urgent operation indeed. Sahari, thank you very much for that. Sahari Ani, their leader of the Red Cross Singapore Mission in Hungary, where he is overseeing medical aid distribution for Ukraine war victims.

title: Singapore Red Cross sends 3rd tranche of aid to Gaza
description: The Singapore Red Cross is sending its third tranche of aid worth over 800,000 Singapore dollars to assist affected communities in Gaza. It's working with the Egyptian Red Cross Society to provide food support and procure medical supplies for hospitals and for the first time. It's also sending civilian volunteers to help with the relief efforts. Our food support will see the emergency humanitarian kitchen in North Sinai provide daily meals for at least 7,000 families. Separately, parcels of basic food items such as rice, flour, salt and oil will also be transported into Gaza to support more than 9,000 families. First aid kits, blood pressure monitors and other medical supplies will also be delivered to hospitals in Gaza. These items were requested by the Palestine Red Crescent Society. At a bolster relief operations, one volunteer will be stationed in Egypt for up to two months to oversee coordination efforts. Eight others are currently on a week-long deployment ending this Sunday. In its previous tranches, the Red Cross distributed over 270,000 dollars worth of aid. Most were medical items. It also sent nearly 200 portable water filters. When the Egyptian Red Crescent spoke to us about the humanitarian kitchen, we were quite supportive of the idea because we can see that this is something that will not only serve the current needs, but it is something that will serve the long-term needs. And the ability to prepare the meals will also be a saving for them because instead of buying prepared meals. So we think that it is a long-term solution. And here to share more is Benjamin William. He is Secretary General and CEO of the Singapore Red Cross. Mr William, it's good to see you. Thank you. Thank you for having me. Talk to me about why there are civilian volunteers being sent this time around, especially we do know that they come from different backgrounds. We understand they have gone through some training. We'll talk about that in a bit. But why civilian volunteers now? So for the Singapore Red Cross over the years, we have trained a pool of overseas disaster responders. So in most crisis, at some stage we will deploy our volunteers whether in terms of overseeing relief supplies or medical interventions or water and sanitation. Now in the case of this response to Gaza, the deployment has taken a bit longer because understandably the situation is very complex. Even getting the permits to be stationed in Cairo in Egypt has taken a while for the approvals to come through. But it has always been our plans to deploy our staff and volunteers to monitor our assistance as we always do in our crisis response. Right. So you mentioned the fact that they've had to apply for permits specifically to actually reach the areas that you want them to get to. Was there a screening process for this? Yes. First of all, we have to work through the Egyptian Red Crescent Society. And the Egyptian Red Crescent Society has to support the volunteers that we have chosen. And so we have supplied the details to them. And they will have to give the assurance to the issuing authorities for the necessary visas. We also of course had the support of the Singapore Embassy in Cairo endorsing our team. And this helped to secure the visas. The point is not of course to put them in any harm's way at all. But will there be a need to ensure their safety? So we are always very careful when we deploy our volunteers and our staff on the ground. And in this case it's even more so. So we have taken all the necessary measures. They are currently deployed in areas which are not in the direct conflict zone. In any case, foreigners cannot go into Gaza. So they are working in Cairo. And the humanitarian kitchen that we talked about is closer to the border. But it's still in a safe zone. That's number one. Number two, we are in very close contact with the Egyptian Red Crescent Society. And the team will always be accompanied by our local partners. Number three, we always have a team of volunteers in Singapore monitoring the situation. Especially the situation in areas where our volunteers are being deployed. And if we get any sense that they are in danger, we will withdraw them from the area either to a safe destination or if need be, back to Singapore. So this is a team of two teams of four in each team. Is that correct? So normally one of our teams is about four persons, four to five persons. But in this case, we have deployed eight members in the team, not counting the one who is staying for one to two months. And so you can consider it's two teams, but they are, you know, doing the same work. The reason is because besides coordinating the relief supplies, working with the Egyptian Red Crescent to ensure that they are loaded on the, they are packed and then they are loaded on the trucks and make their way into Gaza. The Egyptian Red Crescent has also worked with us to, for this process, whereby we are the ones who will work with the suppliers and procure the items directly and give the items to the Egyptian Red Crescent. This way we cut out the middleman administration costs and things like that and we can maximize where our funds go. It also helps the Egyptian Red Crescent Society because they don't have to deal with all the administrative details. We get the supplies. And that's why you need a bigger team on the ground to work all these processes. Getting the aid to the people who need it. That's the essential part of this, right? But we also understand there's a backlog of these aid trucks that are going into Gaza. Does that play into the coordination with the Egyptian Red Crescent as well? You know, in order to expedite, is there a way of expediting the process or is there the ability to actually sort of, as you say, you want to maximize the effort so you're cutting out some of the delay as it were. So having a team on the ground, of course, helps. Part of the role that the team is playing is also assisting in the packing of the items and all that. This relationship with the Egyptian Red Crescent Society is very important. They see us as our partners, as partners being on the ground with them, walking the talk with them. And I think this helps us in also coordinating which items get put on the truck. But over and above that, priorities on the ground change very quickly. And having a team on the ground help us to understand, for example, in the next trench, what should we focus on? You know, we have people coming to say, can we give this and that? And those items may be needed. But it is very clear from Egyptian Red Crescent and other partners on the ground that currently what is needed is food, water and medical supply. So right now we are focused on that. But the next trench might be something else. And having people on the ground help us to coordinate this and make us relevant. If we supply something that is not top priority, it will get delayed and it will be pushed to a later truck. So the situation is changing all the time. That has to always be closely monitored very quickly before we wrap. Mr. William, there are other plans though to send more volunteers at all and perhaps for longer deployments. Yes. So in terms of our coordinator, we will have a coordinator on the ground. And when his term ends, we may send another coordinator, especially if we embark on another trench. With this ongoing crisis and the crisis getting worse and worse, we hope that the Singapore community will come forward to support more funding and we expect to send more teams because we want to make sure that the assistance that Singapore Red Cross is providing goes where it is supposed to go and we help in the process as well. So we do plan to send further teams. Mr. William, we congratulate you and the Singapore Red Cross for the important work that you're doing and all the best with this going forward as well. Thank you very much. Benjamin William, the Secretary-General and CEO of the Singapore Red Cross.

First aid kits, blood pressure monitors and other medical supplies will also be delivered to hospitals in Gaza. These items were requested by the Palestine Red Crescent Society. At a bolster relief operations, one volunteer will be stationed in Egypt for up to two months to oversee coordination efforts. Eight others are currently on a week-long deployment ending this Sunday. We'll talk about that in a bit. But why civilian volunteers now? So for the Singapore Red Cross over the years, we have trained a pool of overseas disaster responders. So in most crisis, at some stage we will deploy our volunteers whether in terms of overseeing relief supplies or medical interventions or water and sanitation. Even getting the permits to be stationed in Cairo in Egypt has taken a while for the approvals to come through. But it has always been our plans to deploy our staff and volunteers to monitor our assistance as we always do in our crisis response. Right. And so we have supplied the details to them. And they will have to give the assurance to the issuing authorities for the necessary visas. We also of course had the support of the Singapore Embassy in Cairo endorsing our team. And this helped to secure the visas. The point is not of course to put them in any harm's way at all. But will there be a need to ensure their safety? So we are always very careful when we deploy our volunteers and our staff on the ground. And in this case it's even more so. Number two, we are in very close contact with the Egyptian Red Crescent Society. And the team will always be accompanied by our local partners. Number three, we always have a team of volunteers in Singapore monitoring the situation. Especially the situation in areas where our volunteers are being deployed. But in this case, we have deployed eight members in the team, not counting the one who is staying for one to two months. And so you can consider it's two teams, but they are, you know, doing the same work. The Egyptian Red Crescent has also worked with us to, for this process, whereby we are the ones who will work with the suppliers and procure the items directly and give the items to the Egyptian Red Crescent. This way we cut out the middleman administration costs and things like that and we can maximize where our funds go. It also helps the Egyptian Red Crescent Society because they don't have to deal with all the administrative details. We get the supplies. And that's why you need a bigger team on the ground to work all these processes. Getting the aid to the people who need it. That's the essential part of this, right? But we also understand there's a backlog of these aid trucks that are going into Gaza. Does that play into the coordination with the Egyptian Red Crescent as well? You know, in order to expedite, is there a way of expediting the process or is there the ability to actually sort of, as you say, you want to maximize the effort so you're cutting out some of the delay as it were. So having a team on the ground, of course, helps. Part of the role that the team is playing is also assisting in the packing of the items and all that. This relationship with the Egyptian Red Crescent Society is very important. They see us as our partners, as partners being on the ground with them, walking the talk with them. And I think this helps us in also coordinating which items get put on the truck. But over and above that, priorities on the ground change very quickly. And having a team on the ground help us to understand, for example, in the next trench, what should we focus on? You know, we have people coming to say, can we give this and that? And those items may be needed. But it is very clear from Egyptian Red Crescent and other partners on the ground that currently what is needed is food, water and medical supply. So right now we are focused on that. But the next trench might be something else. And having people on the ground help us to coordinate this and make us relevant. If we supply something that is not top priority, it will get delayed and it will be pushed to a later truck. So the situation is changing all the time. That has to always be closely monitored very quickly before we wrap. Mr. William, there are other plans though to send more volunteers at all and perhaps for longer deployments. Yes. So in terms of our coordinator, we will have a coordinator on the ground. And when his term ends, we may send another coordinator, especially if we embark on another trench. With this ongoing crisis and the crisis getting worse and worse, we hope that the Singapore community will come forward to support more funding and we expect to send more teams because we want to make sure that the assistance that Singapore Red Cross is providing goes where it is supposed to go and we help in the process as well. So we do plan to send further teams. Mr. William, we congratulate you and the Singapore Red Cross for the important work that you're doing and all the best with this going forward as well. Thank you very much. Benjamin William, the Secretary-General and CEO of the Singapore Red Cross.

title: 2004 tsunami： Singapore Red Cross credits response as pivotal learning lesson
description: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami also provided pivotal learning experience for the Singapore Red Cross, shaping its approach to disaster relief to this day. A key commitment is rapid deployment as it aims to be on the ground within 48 to 72 hours of a crisis. Now to ensure swift action, it has established pre-allocated funds for the immediate deployment of resources. I'll leave Amshia with this report. Life was shattered as nature's wrath descended upon coastal cities across the region, leaving behind an unparalleled trail of death and devastation. In a race against time, the Singapore Red Cross sprang into action, deploying teams to Indonesia and Sri Lanka with precision and effort that required seamless coordination. The immediate response is important in terms of relief items, the immediate relief, trying to see whether we can provide the essentials, water, food, shelter. Subsequent to it, we also have to decide what are the immediate needs on the ground beyond the basic necessities. Back home, an army of volunteers was mobilised to manage the overwhelming flow of donations pouring in, working tirelessly to sort, pack and ensure the aid reached those in desperate need. As the initial chaos began to subside, a sobering realisation set in. Relief efforts would not be a matter of days or weeks but could stretch on for months. This volunteer grasped the profound importance of the mission, dedicating nearly a year in Indonesia to extend a helping hand. The Singapore Red Cross says the lessons learned during those efforts profoundly influenced how they carried out future missions, including its swift and coordinated response to Japan's devastating tsunami in 2011. In order to be able to make sure that the funds we raise are used most efficiently. So we didn't get caught in this mindset that we have to work with the Red Cross, Red Crescent partners only. So we work very closely with the governments. Yeah, we always kept our partners informed of who we are working with. But because of that, we managed to do some major projects in Japan. And that approach proved pivotal for the Singapore Red Cross in 2015, following a devastating earthquake in Nepal. Collaborating with numerous partners, it raised some 13 million dollars. And those contributions became a beacon of hope. Not only did they fund over 40 rebuilding projects, but they also played a key role in restoring the spirit of the people.

title: New blood bank opens in Punggol
description: A new blood bank has opened in Pongol, it's Singapore's fifth blood bank and it's in line with the nation's strategy to locate blood collection centres close to where people live and work. The Health Sciences Authority says with the area's younger population, the new blood bank's location could help recruit more youth donors. This will help meet demand, which is said to grow by more than 30 per cent by 2030. 34-year-old Saraswati Devi has been a blood donor for nearly 20 years. She used to donate at the blood bank in Uchum. But this new one in Pongol, that's closer to her home, means she can cut down on travelling time. It's really convenient because it helps to save me a lot of travel time and it also helps in accommodating to schedule in an appointment easily to donate blood. The Health Sciences Authority says about 21 per cent of blood donors last year were residents in the northeast region. It includes Pongol and nearby towns like Sengkang, which is home to more than 900,000 residents and a relatively young population. It's hoped that the proximity of the new blood bank to this segment could encourage them to come forward. Speaking at its opening, Health Minister Oinkang says Singapore must consistently strive to meet the demand for blood. Each of us can be part of this gift of life. Today we use about 120,000 units of blood a year with a super-agent population and increased healthcare needs. We expect this to go up to beyond 160,000 units of blood per year by 2030. Steps have also been taken to cultivate a sustainable pool of regular blood donors. For instance, the Singapore Red Cross has partnered the Singapore Institute of Technology to promote blood donation drives. Through EDMs, through publicity, we certainly will make use of all available channels to bring the message out and draw people to the blood bank. And these efforts are key during critical periods where blood stocks run low. We're joined by Benjamin William, he's CEO and Secretary General of the Singapore Red Cross and Dr Kam Weesyong, Assistant Group Director of Blood Supply at the Blood Services Group at the Health Sciences Authority. Welcome gentlemen, thanks for coming in this evening. Thanks for having us. I'll start with you, Dr Kam. This idea, we just heard that if we put blood collecting centres closer to where people live and work, they are more likely to give blood, suggesting that if it's convenient, they will do so. And not that people give blood because they have real sustained deep conviction that they should do so. So depending on what you assume, the decentralization of blood collection will increase the amount of blood you collect. Is that so? Are people very committed or not so committed to donating blood? So I can say that the decentralization strategy in Singapore has worked well for us, right? Today is a landmark day for us. We opened our fifth blood bank, Blood Bank in Wampungo. So we already have one in Woodlands, one in Jurong East, one in Dobigot, and obviously one in Blood Bank at HSA in Uchun. So we already have five blood banks and we're making it very convenient now for donors to donate blood. So our strategy is really to reach out to the donors, right? Because we want to serve the communities. So that's one strategy. We make it convenient for them. We understand that Singaporeans are very busy, right? You know, time is of the essence. We understand that. So to make it easy for them to donate blood, we reach out to them. Not only through the blood banks, we also have mobiles, of course. Now then comes the other strategy which we're working on now. We want to consolidate our donor pool, right? The next strategy, the next space we are at now is really to get these donors to come to our blood banks. So which is why today we launched our initiative, Adopt the Blood Bank Initiative. So by reaching out to the donors through our five blood banks, and now we are trying to channel them to the blood banks through the Adopt the Blood Bank Initiative. So these two strategies will work in synergy. Adopt the blood bank. Adopt the blood bank. Okay. So we want corporate offices, schools, you know, all these organizations to really adopt the blood bank and own the blood bank and then they can channel their staff, you know, the students. And today you heard from Singapore Institute of Technology. So we're working very closely through partnership with Singapore Red Cross. Yeah, so let's bring you in here now, Mr. Williams. So I believe our blood donation rate in Singapore is about 1.8% of the population. So compared to other developed countries like UK and Australia, which is around like two to three percent, what is it going to take for Singapore to get there? I mean, with this additional blood bank in Pongol, I mean, what kind of numbers are you expecting to hit? Yeah. So right now the percentage of population that donates annually is about 1.8%. We need to get it up and for several reasons, and particularly because of the aging population. So over and above what Dr. Kham has said, I think the decentralization policy is very important also for our changing the psyche in Singapore that blood donation must be a national responsibility. You know, we cannot just leave it to 1.8% of the population to bear the load. We need to reach out to more. So we need to increase the overall pool of blood donors. But given that Singapore is an aging population and Minister Ong used the term super-agent population, we need to increase our pool of youth donors. Currently the percentage of youth donors is only 17%. My goal is to see it increase to about 30% or more. That is the only way we can have a sustainable pool of blood donors in the longer term. By when about 30% you said from 70 to 30? I think we are taking considerable action over the next say about 3 to 5 years to increase this. And one of the major strategies is adopt the blood bank. What is adopt the blood bank means? You know, we now have organizations that organize blood mobiles. But that's once a year. Adopting the blood bank means that you come on board to say that you feel a responsibility to make this blood bank work. And decentralization dovetails very nicely into this strategy. So you have one Punggol today. But you have a Singapore Institute of Technology as a neighbor. You have Sokak as a neighbor. These organizations will find it easier to identify with this blood bank and say we want to adopt it. So for example, we have SMU which is next to Dovicott Blood Bank. So that's how we want to get more people to come on board. Not just say, okay, I'll do a blood mobile once a year. But regularly be there to promote the blood bank to get their employees to... It could be clear about the link. So for example, say if it's close to SMU, where I take, given the large student population, I suppose young people at that age would be more interested in giving back more progressively, maybe relatively progressive in their ideas. So if they adopt a blood bank, what is their responsibility to that blood bank that would make it more likely that you will see more young people giving more blood over a sustained period of time? So I think one of the things that we find in young people today and you is that they believe in a cause. So I think it is very important to bring them on board to believe that blood donation is a national life-saving cause. Dr Kham, your response to that? I definitely agree with Sajjan. I think we want to make this a national... That's the psyche, yes? We want to make it a lifestyle, a culture, a habit. So how do we make that happen? You know, we need to engage the youth donors. So for example, just this year at the World Blood Donor Day, we introduced a new award category to acknowledge and recognize that contribution. So we have this award called the Youthphoria Award and we have youth donors actually donating a lot of times to receive the award. So that's one way we want to get the message out that, hey, you know what? Youth donors can also contribute to the National Blood Program. They can do a lot of things. And I think the challenge is really engage... How do we engage this group of donors? How do we get them to come on board with us? And you mentioned you're trying to change mindsets and the psyche, which is quite a tough task. And now that you have a fifth blood bank, just looking ahead, what are some of the other plans in the pipeline, you know, just to attract not just the youth, but you mentioned about organizations as well, companies and firms. Could you just touch on that? So maybe I'll ask. So one of the major initiatives is, besides the individual donors, is to work with organizations. So one big group that we are hoping to get on board and we have made considerable progress is the grassroots organizations. So the idea is that we want to have a constant reminder, for example, in our community centers that blood donation is important. So this will reach the bigger pool. Likewise, we are working on a similar initiative in the Institutes of Higher Learning and Tertiary Institutions to have a constant reminder in each of these campuses, sort of a blood booth, giving information on blood donation, reminding people that blood donation is such a critical part of total defense and resilient community. And I think we need to keep this constant. Maybe if I can add as well. I think specifically for the youth group, the youth donors, we've, you know, engaged them in various measures. For example, we use social media now. Of course, Singapore Red Cross, we have an Instagram account, a blood buddy account. We use Facebook. So we're trying to use media, social media to appeal to them. And also, we've also make it very convenient for them. You know, nowadays, youth donors are very digital savvy. So we've launched the Donate Blood app, making it so convenient. Just download the app, undergo. They can make an appointment. They can fill up the donor questionnaire. It will make it very easy to them. So we're moving towards, you know, digitalizing our processes to really make it easy and engaging for our donors to come and donate blood. Alright, so an attack on all fronts. Yeah, because it's a no option. You know, we actually do not have an option other than increasing our pool of young donors and youth donors because in the long term, we will be a super-agent population. And not the long term, 2030, we are talking about. Yeah, and you want to raise it to what? Grow my more than 30% by 2030. Thanks so much. Benjamin William, from the Singapore Red Cross, and Dr. Kamui Siong from HSA. Thanks so much for joining us. Thank you.

title: COVID-19： Donations to Singapore Red Cross' relief operations in China hit S$6m
description: Donations for Singapore Red Cross' relief operations in China have hit $6 million. The money will go to help healthcare workers and patients affected by the COVID-19 outbreak. More than $2 million will be used to supply essential equipment like protection goggles, face shields and respiratory humidifiers. The supplies will be sent to three hospitals in Wuhan and seven social welfare homes in two other cities. Specialist ambulances will be sent in the next phase. If some items are already made in China, money will be sent instead. We always adopt a policy where our funding goes in tranches. They give us reports on the ground of the project being completed. They are assured that the goods have been distributed where they are supposed to go. Then we follow up with another tranche of payment. Separately, the Health Sciences Authority has also given an update on the national blood supply in Singapore. It reached critically low levels last week as donors stayed away because of virus fears. But the situation has improved due to public appeals. Donations were up by around 70 per cent over the weekend and on Monday, but are still not yet in healthy range. HSA is urging more donors to come forward. It says there are precautions in place to keep donors safe. The authority adds there's no evidence for now that COVID-19 can be transmitted through blood. Donors are only allowed to enter the clinics after being screened.

title: Blood donation： Blood stock may drop to ＂critical levels＂ during festive period, says SRC
description: A Singapore's blood stock could dip to critical levels this festive period, and this could lead to postponement of surgeries and essential treatments. The Singapore Red Cross is calling for more donors as demand is rising faster than supply. Aslam Shah with more. Just this one bag can save up to three lives. And supplying it has been a routine for 34-year-old Lance Lai. His father had brought him to donate during his polytechnic days, and he has visited the blood bank every year since. It process very fast and seamless, so why not just come down and try, do a part of the day to give it a community and have a safe life. But current blood donors like Lance represent just about 1.9% of the population, a percentage that the Singapore Red Cross is keen to boost. Lance says he struggles to get his peers on board as they cite lack of time and have misconceptions about safety. Donations are key, especially amid the Chinese New Year holidays. When blood banks close and supplies freeze, even as demand continues to be high. This is why it's crucial to replenish the stock once donation resumes on Friday. It will become a challenge for us if there is a reduce of donors. Our main concern here is the youth donors. The regular donors, and generally we have a very good pool of donors who are 35 and above. But at some point of time, maybe due to age or medical problems, they might not be able to donate blood. Then we have to rely on the youth donors. So I think the youths need to step up and come forward to donate blood. The old blood type remains both in demand, as almost half the population has this blood type. Bloods' shelf life only lasts about 42 days. With a surge in overseas travel during this festive season, donations may be affected as travelers may need to go through a wait-out period of up to 4 months upon return. To help boost immediate supply, SRC has a 2-day blood donation drive at North Point City in Yixuan from Friday. It plans to further ramp up donation drives this year.
